method: The load is the number of devices multiplied by the draw per device in watts. The per-port limit is the switch-side (PSE) power of the selected standard: 15.4 W for 802.3af Type 1, 30 W for 802.3at Type 2, 60 W for 802.3bt Type 3 and 90 W for 802.3bt Type 4, and a device draw above that limit is rejected rather than silently clamped. Devices supported by power is the switch budget divided by the draw per device and rounded down; devices supported by ports is simply the port count, so the switch can power the smaller of the two and the limiting factor is reported as power, ports, or balanced when the two are equal. Spare headroom is the budget minus the load, and a negative value marks the plan as over budget with the shortfall shown; a device count above the port count reports the extra ports needed. The budget accepts 0.1 to 10000 W, ports 1 to 512, devices 1 to 1024 and a draw from 0.1 to 90 W, with at most two decimals for watts and whole numbers for counts. Cable loss is not modelled: the standards reserve about 2.5 W per port, which is why a 15.4 W port guarantees roughly 12.95 W at a device 100 m away. Per-port class negotiation, redundancy, inrush current and thermal derating are also out of scope. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: IEEE 802.3af-2003, Data Terminal Equipment (DTE) Power via Media Dependent Interface: 15.4 W at the PSE and 12.95 W at the powered device.
IEEE 802.3at-2009, Power over Ethernet enhancements: Type 2 supplies 30 W at the PSE and 25.5 W at the powered device.
IEEE 802.3bt-2018, Power over Ethernet over four pairs: Type 3 supplies 60 W and Type 4 supplies 90 W at the PSE.
